newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam economist calls for new wave of reforms.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam economist calls for new wave of reforms.

text.p: A leading economist in Ho Chi Minh City on Friday called for a new wave of reforms aimed at reviving Vietnam's economy and providing for sustainable future development.

Pham Xuan Ai, of the Ho Chi Minh City Economic Institute told the Thoi Bao Kinh Te Sai Gon newspaper in an interview that Vietnam's decade-old economic renovation process, known as Doi Moi, had reached a point of near exhaustion.
"It's time for the state to work out policies to bring Vietnam's economy into a new period," he said. "Maybe slower, but more sustainable."
Ai said government leaders were right in focusing their efforts on boosting flagging industrial output, but said the consumer market had suffered as a consequence of being ignored for too long.

He added that recent troubles in the banking system and the failure of the state to mobilise idle domestic capital from under the floorboards of Vietnam's 77 million population, had also emerged as problems which needed to be overcome.

Ai's comments follow the recent emergence of what some see as a series of "mini-crises" in the economy, and the first real downturn since Hanoi dropped its Soviet-style command-led system in favour of free-market capitalism in the late 1980s.
He said the current slowdown should be viewed as a normal cyclical phenomenon, but added: "The time for broad development is over. Now we have to add depth to that development."
Ai said the government should attempt to use inflation to promote consumer spending, to create additional capital for industry, and to help with the export competitiveness of Vietnamese goods.
But he also emphasised that inflation should be "controlled but not restricted" and said efforts were also needed to encourage investment.
The full extent of Vietnam's current slowdown is difficult to assess, chiefly because of an absence of reliable information.
Gross domestic product (GDP) growth in 1996 was put at 9.34 percent, although some foreign economists say the figure is misleading and may in reality lie between five and seven percent.
Government officials have indicated that this year's GDP growth will be lower than in 1996. In addition they say foreign direct investment levels are down.
According to figures published recently in the official press the first seven months of this year saw a 25 percent slide in investment from overseas.
Government sources indicate however this may be just the tip of an iceberg and report a far higher figure showing a more drastic decline, put at between 50 and 60 percent.

Ai's remarks echo those of a number of Western economists and diplomats, who have expressed concern about the prolonged absence of new reforms in an economy previously seen as one of the most promising new stars in East Asia.
U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright visited in late June and told Vietnam's leaders what they needed was "a Doi Moi Two".
